meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Laws are Like Sausages. Better Not to See Them Being Made'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Bismarck. Credited to lawyer-poet John Godfrey Saxe in the University Chronicle, 27 March 1869. The Bismarck version first appears in 1933.

answer.label: Not Bismarck — credited to John Godfrey Saxe
answer.authorDates: 1816–1887 · American lawyer-poet, newspaper editor and public lecturer
answer.sourceLine: No German original has ever been traced, and Bismarck was not linked to the quip until 1933 — thirty-five years after his death. The earliest version on record belongs to the American lawyer-poet John Godfrey Saxe, quoted in the University Chronicle of the University of Michigan on 27 March 1869: “Laws, like sausages, cease to inspire respect in proportion as we know how they are made.” The snappy modern one-liner is a later condensation of that sentence, not anyone’s documented words — Quote Investigator ↗.

source.excerpt: “Laws,” says that illustrious rhymer, Mr. John Godfrey Saxe, “like sausages, cease to inspire respect in proportion as we know how they are made;” and we fancy it is much the same with impeachment trials.
trail: 27 March 1869 — the earliest appearance located by Quote Investigator ↗: the University Chronicle at the University of Michigan quotes “that illustrious rhymer, Mr. John Godfrey Saxe” on laws, sausages and respect.

29 March 1869 — the Daily Cleveland Herald carries the same line credited to Saxe. Fred Shapiro reported this cite for the Yale Book of Quotations and concluded it “may be the true origin of the saying,” as quoted by Quote Investigator ↗.
1933 — the first known link to Bismarck, in Claudius O. Johnson’s textbook Government in the United States, and even there it is a guess: “I think it was Bismarck who said…” (Quote Investigator ↗).
Today — Wikiquote ↗ lists the saying in its Misattributed section for Bismarck, pointing to the same 1869 University Chronicle citation for Saxe.
source.excerptNote: This is the earliest appearance Quote Investigator has located. Note what it is and is not: a newspaper quoting Saxe in passing, applied to an impeachment trial. It is not the pithy modern sentence, and it is not Bismarck.

source.rightsNote: No rights status is claimed for the popular wording — “Laws are like sausages. It’s better not to see them being made” is an anonymous twentieth-century condensation with no identified author or first publication, so there is nothing to date. The 1869 sentence reproduced above is a different matter: it was printed in the University Chronicle at Ann Arbor on 27 March 1869 and in the Daily Cleveland Herald two days later, both far outside any surviving US copyright term.

author.name: John Godfrey Saxe
author.kicker: The man who actually said it
author.heading: Who was John Godfrey Saxe?
author.metaLine: 1816–1887 · American lawyer-poet, newspaper editor and lecturer
author.bio: John Godfrey Saxe was a Vermont attorney who became one of nineteenth-century America’s most popular comic poets — admitted to the bar in 1843, State’s Attorney for Chittenden County, and editor of the Burlington Sentinel from 1850 to 1856. He is best remembered today for The Blind Men and the Elephant, but in his own lifetime he was a celebrity of the lecture circuit, and newspapers routinely printed his one-liners as the sayings of “that illustrious rhymer.” That is exactly how the sausage aphorism reaches us: not from a book of his, but from the press quoting him in the spring of 1869.

copyAttribution: "Laws, like sausages, cease to inspire respect in proportion as we know how they are made." — John Godfrey Saxe, quoted in the University Chronicle (University of Michigan), 27 March 1869. Not Otto von Bismarck: no German source exists and the Bismarck attribution first appears in 1933, thirty-five years after his death. Via Quotle.info

misattribution.heading: Who gets credit, and who earned it
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most confidently misquoted lines in political English. Three separate things have gone wrong with it: the speaker, the century, and the words.

items.why: Bismarck (1815–1898) is credited almost universally, but no German original has ever been produced and the attribution post-dates his death by decades. The earliest Bismarck citation Quote Investigator ↗ can find is a 1933 textbook that hedges with “I think it was Bismarck.” The Oxford Dictionary of Quotations files the line under Misquotations with the verdict “attributed to Bismarck, but not traced and probably apocryphal,” and Wikiquote ↗ lists it as Misattributed.

items.who: Nobody — the familiar wording is orphaned
items.why: Saxe’s attested sentence is longer and more interesting: laws “cease to inspire respect in proportion as we know how they are made.” The clipped versions in circulation — “better not to see them being made,” “to retain respect for sausages and laws, one must not watch them in the making” — are later compressions that Professor Buzzkill ↗ describes as having lost the original’s analytical edge. No source document for the popular one-liner has been identified.

The thought is older than Saxe. Quote Investigator ↗ traces a French version printed in 1798 in L’Esprit des Journaux — one risks disgust on seeing how administration, justice and dinner are prepared — which Chamfort himself credited to a witty advocate named Marchand, though later printings dropped that acknowledgement. It is an ancestor of the idea, not the source of the English sentence.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest credit line is John Godfrey Saxe, on the strength of contemporary newspaper attributions from March 1869 — a conclusion reached independently by Fred Shapiro and Ralph Keyes and set out in full by Quote Investigator ↗, which advises crediting Saxe rather than Bismarck.

context.heading: Why this one travelled so far
lead: It is the perfect political aphorism: short, cynical, and flattering to whoever repeats it. It is also the perfect misattribution — an American joke about legislatures, transplanted onto the most quotable statesman of the nineteenth century, decades after he was dead.

The transplant is documented. Quote Investigator’s earliest Bismarck citation is a 1933 university textbook, Government in the United States by Claudius O. Johnson, whose chapter on congressional procedure opens with a shrug: “I think it was Bismarck who said that the man who wishes to keep his respect for sausages and laws should not see how either is made.” Later writers dropped the hedge. By 1958 an Ogden, Utah newspaper could call it “an old saying attributed to Prince Bismarck” without blinking.
context.detailsSummary: The sausage duel that may have made the swap feel right
detailsBody: Quote Investigator raises one further possibility, flagged there as speculative: Bismarck was already publicly associated with sausages. A widely reprinted anecdote — located by QI in a South Carolina newspaper, The Mountaineer, on 18 July 1867 — has Bismarck challenging the pathologist Rudolf Virchow to a duel, and Virchow, then studying trichinosis, choosing sausages as the weapons: one infected, one clean, with Bismarck to take his pick at breakfast.

Whether or not that yarn greased the misattribution, it explains why “Bismarck” and “sausage” sat comfortably in the same sentence for readers long before anyone credited him with the aphorism itself.
context.pull: Bismarck died in 1898. The first person to put this line in his mouth did so in 1933.

sourcesVerified.claim: The earliest citation attributing a version of the quotation to Otto von Bismarck is a 1933 textbook, 'Government in the United States' by Claudius O. Johnson, p. 321, which hedges: 'I think it was Bismarck who said that the man who wishes to keep his respect for sausages and laws should not see how either is made.'

QI located a 27 March 1869 cite in the University Chronicle (University of Michigan), p. 4, Ann Arbor: '"Laws," says that illustrious rhymer, Mr. John Godfrey Saxe, "like sausages, cease to inspire respect in proportion as we know how they are made;" and we fancy it is much the same with impeachment trials.'

Fred Shapiro (Freakonomics blog, updating the Yale Book of Quotations) wrote that Bismarck 'was not associated with that quip until the 1930's' and that the Daily Cleveland Herald of 29 March 1869 quoted John Godfrey Saxe, which 'may be the true origin of the saying'; Ralph Keyes found a Saxe attribution of 29 April 1869 (The Quote Verifier, 2006, pp. 188, 324).

The Oxford Dictionary of Quotations lists 'Laws are like sausages. It's better not to see them being made' in its Misquotations section with the note 'attributed to Bismarck, but not traced and probably apocryphal'; and QI concludes the questioner should credit John Godfrey Saxe instead of Otto von Bismarck.

QI reports a 1958 Ogden Standard-Examiner (Ogden, Utah) line: 'There is an old saying attributed to Prince Bismarck that "to retain respect for sausages and laws, one must not watch them in the making"'; and a 18 July 1867 anecdote in The Mountaineer (Greenville, South Carolina) about a proposed Bismarck–Virchow duel with sausages as weapons.

Wikiquote lists the laws-and-sausages saying in its Misattributed section for Otto von Bismarck, gives the earliest known version as John Godfrey Saxe's, cites the University Chronicle (University of Michigan), 27 March 1869, and notes such remarks only began being attributed to Bismarck in the 1930s.

The Wikiquote talk page discussion records that no German-language source for the saying was found, that searches of JSTOR, Lexis-Nexis and Google Books turned up nothing supporting Bismarck, that an earlier attribution to John Godfrey Saxe was found in an 1869 Michigan publication, and that the concept traces back to Nicolas de Chamfort.

Professor Buzzkill's verdict is that there is no evidence Bismarck ever said it, that the idea was attributed to American poet John Godfrey Saxe (1816-1887) as early as 1869 in the University Chronicle, University of Michigan, 27 March 1869, and that the version was only attributed to Bismarck in the 1930s.

John Godfrey Saxe lived 2 June 1816 to 31 March 1887, was an American poet, attorney, newspaper editor and lecturer, admitted to the Vermont bar in 1843, State's Attorney for Chittenden County 1850-1852, and editor of the Burlington Sentinel 1850-1856.
Otto von Bismarck was born 1 April 1815 and died 30 July 1898, serving as Minister President of Prussia from 1862 and as Chancellor of the German Empire from 1871 to 1890.

Google Books holds a full-view record for University Chronicle, Volume 3 — the volume Quote Investigator cites for the 27 March 1869 Saxe attestation. (The record confirms the volume's identity; the page-4 snippet itself was not reproduced in the fetched page.)

Quote Investigator documents a French precursor printed in 1798 in L'Esprit des Journaux — 'On court les risques du dégoût en voyant comment l'administration, la justice & la cuisine se préparent' — which Chamfort attributed to a witty advocate named Marchand, and links it as a similar remark to the laws-and-sausages saying.
The Internet Archive holds a full scan of 'The poems of John Godfrey Saxe' by Saxe, John Godfrey (1816-1887), published 1872 by J. Osgood, Boston, catalogued NOT_IN_COPYRIGHT.
